title: Reaching for the phone, sensing presence, talking to the dead, and continuing bonds

source_packet.source_basis: Public-source afterward/bereavement/funeral-language synthesis for schema testing; no private testimony, no individual legal, financial, funeral, clinical, mental-health, or ritual advice.
limitations: Public sources support broad vocabulary and practical context only; they do not supply consented room texture.
This record must not become legal, estate, financial, funeral, clinical, mental-health, diagnosis, ritual, or crisis advice.
Local law, institutional policy, funeral-home/cemetery/crematory requirements, clinicians, mental-health professionals, guardians, tradition holders, and the person’s wishes govern actual decisions.

moment.plain_scene: A bereaved person reaches to call the person who died, speaks aloud to them, feels guided by them, keeps a place for them, writes messages, visits a grave, or maintains a relationship in altered form.
ordinary_language_queries: I keep reaching to call my dead mom
is it normal to talk to the dead

content_layers.observation_text: A bereaved person reaches to call the person who died, speaks aloud to them, feels guided by them, keeps a place for them, writes messages, visits a grave, or maintains a relationship in altered form.
content_layers.source_synthesis: HFA describes non-linear grief and memory triggers; Hospiscare summarizes the continuing-bonds model as maintaining connection rather than assuming healthy grief requires detachment. This record is not a diagnostic or spiritual claim.

interpretation.editor_interpretation: The archive should preserve the relational afterlife of the dead in ordinary behavior: phone reach, recipes, jokes, grave visits, text threads, dreams, habits, and private speech.

what_this_is_not: not a claim that continuing bonds are necessary or comforting for everyone
not a replacement for support if experiences are frightening, impairing, or unsafe
uncertainties: Continuing bonds may comfort, distress, change over time, or be unwanted.
Cultural and religious frames shape whether talking to the dead is ordinary, sacred, taboo, or pathological.
Clinical support may be needed when grief becomes disabling or unsafe.
content_layers.lay_orientation: A lay surface should make the phrase findable, orient the reader to why the moment is common enough to name, and then stop before giving personal legal, financial, funeral, mental-health, clinical, or ritual advice.
content_layers.practitioner_notes: A practitioner or researcher surface should collect who had authority, what words were used, what the setting required, what the family understood, where conflict or exclusion appeared, and which local/professional supports were involved.
language_notes: Do not treat grief as a stage, task, timetable, performance, or disorder unless a qualified diagnostic context exists.
Keep legal, funeral, financial, child, and ritual content jurisdiction- and authority-bound.
Preserve ordinary words the bereaved use, including euphemism, anger, numbness, absence, and administrative speech.
